What I'm asking for is consistency: Either the super build handles all the dependencies, or it handles none and they are documented. I think removing the automation you already have would however be a mistake. It makes it convenient. If you simply add the git submodules update to the super build you're already done.

I wouldn't spend too much energy on trying to find the perfect solution. Do it one way, make it consistent and make sure the documentation is clear.

title: Mission generation should use NAV_DELAY instead of sending two waypoints on the same location
body:
From @julianoes:
> The reason MAVSDK sends the same lat/lon twice in a row is because it adds a LOITER_TIME right after a NAV_WAYPOINT. The right approach would be to use NAV_DELAY [...].

Which is implemented in PX4 for quite some time (I verified). The reason PX4 rejects now waypoints that are on top of each other is because the path between those waypoints is not defined (zero distance). Often we however need to know where the vehicle is coming from geometrically and allowing N waypoints on the same location would force us to traverse the mission multiple times and quite a bit forward and backward, increasing the complexity of the autopilot in terms of memory, execution time and also in terms of our ability to QA and certify the code.

So in short: This is undesirable in principle and navigation commands should not exist in the same physical location one after the other.

comments.body:
> So in short: This is undesirable in principle and navigation commands should not exist in the same physical location one after the other.

If this is a hard rule it should also be added to the MAVLink standard.

There are a couple of scenarios that cannot be done if there is such a hard rule:
(PREVIOUS WAYPOINT), WAYPOINT, DELAY, IMAGE_START_CAPTURE, LOITER_UNLIMITED for example if the waypoint and loiter_unlimited have the same position. We could prevent this reverse transversing if all the mission items in such a sequence would have the same PREVIOUS WAYPOINT assigned.
@dayjaby I suppose for this case we should be using WAYPOINT, DELAY, IMAGE_START_CAPTURE, DELAY, but maybe that's not possible given the current implementation.

title: Who should initiate TIMESYNC?
body:
This is related to #1169. Looking at MAVSDK's timesync implementation, it seems like we send TIMESYNC messages in two situations:

1. In `process_timesync`, where we receive a TIMESYNC message and answer to it
2. In `do_work`, where we actually initiate the TIMESYNC exchange

Is it meant to be like this, or do different components have different needs? E.g. the "master" (I would guess the autopilot) could be the one initiating the sync, and he other components may or may not answer depending on their needs, right?

@irsdkv: your insights would be appreciated :slightly_smiling_face:!

comments.body:
This is the same implementation as in MAVROS:

For the FCU to sync, the FCU sends a message and waits for the onboard computer to answer.
For the onboard computer to sync, it sends a message and waits for the FCU's answer.

This could be in tri-way protocol two-way, where the onboard computer sends a request, FCU replies and the onboard answers to the FCU. The onboard computer will have its sync from the 2 first messages, the FCU from the 3 last messages. This would remove one message but add one time to the TIMESYNC message. I do not know it would improve bandwidth.
Mavros implementation:

[Replies]
https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/de9f39a719b091b8448214a17d27b3b1c415d0dc/mavros/src/plugins/sys_time.cpp#L308-L321

[Requests]
https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/de9f39a719b091b8448214a17d27b3b1c415d0dc/mavros/src/plugins/sys_time.cpp#L334-L346


Precision Time Protocol 2: [NOT PX4's version]
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6976744/90625099-59fc7b00-e219-11ea-8277-8522f899d45d.png)

Oh it was a long time ago and unfortunately I don't remember all important details now :(

But @AlexisTM explanation is correct.

Also I would to say that [this code change](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/1169/files#diff-ec4205b6bc1adbc844894d870f234adaR9) disables ability to answer to `TIMESYNC` requests from other devices in common with disabling MAVSDK's own requests.

I think that it is a good idea to save the opportunity to sync time by default in case of other device want to do it.

What are you think about that, @AlexisTM ?

UPD:
Also I think that disabling by default MAVSDK's initiated timesync is not a bad idea, because it is needed only for positioning using external vision for now as I know.

I checked out #1034 and found that it is only way to disable `do_work` and `process_timesync` both simultaneously.

And as @AlexisTM said this functionality really needed only for advanced usage.

So this PR seems like a good choice.

But @JonasVautherin please say why this is a problem to save this functionality enabled by default? Is it add payload or brings some other troubles?

> please say why this is a problem to save this functionality enabled by default?

Because it's not clear to me how TIMESYNC supports more than 2 components doing the synchronization. Hence, if you have more than 2 components, I'm currently assuming that you will have to disable TIMESYNC in the extra ones, and you will have to know which one needs to enable it. In that case, it seems more legit to have it disabled by default IMO.

My reasoning is the following: the TIMESYNC message is a broadcast message (because it doesn't have `target_system` and `target_component`). Therefore, a component cannot know who the message was destined to. So if you have, say, the FCU synchronizing with a module M1 on the companion, and at the same time a module M2 on the companion synchronizing with the ground station, then I can't imagine how the FCU can make the difference between the response coming from M1 (which it is interested in) and the response coming from the ground station (which is destined to M2).

@JonasVautherin I fully agree, this protocol was designed out of necessity for a time synchronization between two devices to allow better control. 

I believe it is useless in most of the use-cases and instead will be a problem to the user if multiple endpoints are connected.

TIMESYNC only works if:
* There are **only** two devices
* The synchronization time is computed & filtered in **each** receiving end (the pixhawk for vision estimation input & the computer for position output)
* The link should be high speed with low jitter, probably only using hardware serial (USB-Serial has up to 20ms spikes)

@AlexisTM Yes. There is a little discussion of this message here: https://github.com/mavlink/mavlink-devguide/issues/194#issuecomment-512037079

And one day I will find time to document it.
I would vote that we make this feature opt-in for use cases where it is required, and supported.
Ok, that answers my question, and TIMESYNC is now disabled by default in MAVSDK. Closing this.

title: Mavlink header install using ExternalProject_Add
body:
When building MAVSDK using CMake's ExternalProject_Add, with SUPERBUILD on, it will properly pull and build all of MAVSDK's dependencies. However, I get errors for missing mavlink headers and indeed [this commit](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/commit/04e78f163d3dd630103a353cca8d04fd943f8486#diff-4c224720c825bc0b47c1375867b1f0eb0f7943639c4ef77d1d7ef38e9792ccb6) changed where the files were installed to. It would be great if we could either have the mavlink headers installed alongside the mavsdk ones automatically, or at least have a CMake option to change where dependencies are installed to.

I would suggest possibly setting `DEPS_INSTALL_PATH` to `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` on [this line]( https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/0338c3e5eb86ec6c00a11ae99b019c97646b907a/CMakeLists.txt#L56) . Alternatively, you could make `DEPS_INSTALL_PATH` an optional argument, so users can place it to their needs, and it would be accessible via ExternalProject_Add.

comments.body:
I wonder if `-DDEPS_INSTALL_PATH` when you build MAVSDK doesn't just allow you to set it. But probably it should rather be an `option()` to make this clear...

Note that in your project that depends on MAVSDK (let's call it `my-project`), you can set the `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` to the install path of the MAVSDK third parties. Something like this:

```cmake
cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="your/cmake/prefix/path;path/to/mavsdk/build/third_party/install" -Bbuild -S.
```

This said, after some experience with CMake superbuilds, my more recent opinion is that we should provide helpers, but not a superbuild (see my blog post [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/)). That's much less confusing in the sense that it makes it clear to the user that they should handle their dependencies.

But well, doesn't change the fact that MAVSDK uses this superbuild, and many users don't want to know about how they should handle their dependencies :see_no_evil:. So probably your best bet is what I wrote in my previous message.

To a degree, yeah, if I wanted to put mavlink specifically into my cmake code. I was trying to keep it generic. When using ExternalProject_Add, the code is not yet in CMake at generation time, so I can't use find_package on a target which is not installed yet. If I pulled the full repo and had it as a submodule instead (before calling any CMake), then yes I could use the CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH.
I somewhat reverted this to the previous behaviour: #2084.

> To a degree, yeah, if I wanted to put mavlink specifically into my cmake code. I was trying to keep it generic.

Well MAVSDK transitively depends on MAVLink in its public interface (before #2084), and therefore `find_package` must find MAVLink somewhere. It's not about "putting mavlink specifically into your cmake code", it won't actually change your CMake code. You just have to tell your CMake project where to find the dependencies with `find_package`. Either you install MAVLink on your system, or you point CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to it.

When you install the MAVSDK `.deb` package, it depends on stuff like openssl, and it will require you to install them on your system. Still you don't consider that you are "putting openssl specifically into your cmake code", right? That's exactly the same for MAVLink, except that MAVLink is not available with `apt install libmavlink-dev`.

> I somewhat reverted this to the previous behaviour: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/2084.

Yeah I guess that solves the confusion around the transitive dependency :+1:

title: Issue of Mission Execution and Manual Input Priority
body:
When the "manual_control.set_manual_control_input"s value keeps changing, I want to execute a mission or other automode. In such a case, the value needs to remain consistent before and after the mission is triggered; otherwise, the mission will be interrupted. However, I’ve noticed that even if I set the manual value right before executing the mission, and then immediately trigger the task, it still gets interrupted. It turns out that I have to wait several hundred milliseconds after setting the value before executing the mission. It seems that the mission has a higher priority, even if the command is input later, the flight controller receives and processes it first.

Then I looked into the source code and found that these two types of commands follow different paths，one goes through a queue, while the other is sent directly as a command. So now I’m wondering: how can I make the information in the queue be delivered faster, so that I don’t have to wait for several hundred milliseconds?

Im current using v3.3.0
Thanks.

comments.body: I'm not following. What are you trying to do and what is the problem exactly? And is this with PX4 or ArduPilot?

@julianoes Im using PX4.
I want to implement the following use case: the drone is originally flying in mission mode, and my onboard vision computer monitors the environment. When an obstacle is detected, it will intervene and interrupt the mission. Once the obstacle is cleared and it's safe to proceed, I want to resume the mission.

The problem lies in resuming the mission. For example, initially I send set_manual_control_input(0, 0, 1, 0) to take control. Then, when I want to hand control back to the mission, I set set_manual_control_input(0, 0, 0.5, 0) and immediately call mission.start_mission(). After that, I continuously send set_manual_control_input(0, 0, 0.5, 0).

However, the resumed mission gets interrupted again right away. I believe this is because the earlier manual control input set_manual_control_input(0, 0, 1, 0) is still considered active by the flight controller. To avoid this, I have to wait a few hundred milliseconds after sending the first set_manual_control_input(0, 0, 0.5, 0) before calling mission.start_mission().

It seems like mission.start_mission() is being sent after but received before the manual control command by the flight controller.

Ok, I think manual_control is not the right interface to do this. Instead, I would pause the mission using `mission_pause` which will go into hold.

Or, alternatively if you want to do some control to avoid the obstacle, I would do that in offboard mode, e.g. using velocity commands.

Manual control is really meant for "manual" as in human control, and not automated control like that.

Also, PX4 implements an interface for obstacle avoidance that we probably should use instead, however, it's not implemented by MAVSDK yet, and I also don't know what the state of it is in PX4, but I do know that it would be the right thing to do, at least long term.

@julianoes Because my drone is a VTOL operating in fixed-wing mode, it cannot hold position in place. So, when an obstacle is detected, I cannot simply switch to a HOLD mode. Instead, the onboard computer must automatically control the drone to fly toward a safe, obstacle-free area and resume mission. Although this is implemented via manual control commands as if a human were flying the drone, it is actually the onboard system issuing the commands autonomously.
I checked PX4's obstacle avoidance feature, and it currently only supports multicopter mode，so I want to implement an onboard computer to interrupt the mission when necessary and resume it when it's safe. But I have to add a delay of several hundred milliseconds  before resuming the mission, which is very troublesome.

Right. I'm afraid I don't have experience with all that.

I'm not 100% understanding your exact issue, but my understanding is that you would always send manual control commands, whether you are in mission or position mode, and then switch the mode between them as you see fit. Have you tried that?
Going to close this. If you have more comments or steps for me to reproduce this, just comment.
